title: The Torah in Greek
hook: the Torah is translated into Greek; legend says by seventy-two elders

segments.voice: Yesterday, Alexander came through like a storm, and in the legend he bowed to the high priest. Your line was two cultures meet. Where did you notice the meeting? Today, the Torah itself crosses into Greek. Day eight hundred eighty-nine.

A king sends for seventy-two elders. That's how the Talmud tells it, in tractate Megillah. King Ptolemy gathers them, and before they can talk to each other, he puts each one in a separate house. He doesn't tell them why. Then he goes to each man alone and says the same thing: write for me the Torah of Moses your teacher. In Greek. Seventy-two rooms. Seventy-two pens. No way to compare notes. If you've ever translated anything, even a text message for a grandparent, here is the problem. A sentence can have more than one right answer. So what comes out of those seventy-two rooms?
screen: `SEVENTY-TWO ELDERS.` → `SEVENTY-TWO SEPARATE HOUSES.` → `WRITE FOR ME THE TORAH.`

segments.voice: The same thing, every time. The Talmud says God put wisdom in each one's heart, and all of them agreed. Even more: each one made the same small changes, in places where a word-for-word Greek version might be misread by a king. The very first line is one of them. Hebrew opens with the word for in the beginning, then created, then God. Read too literally, a Greek reader might think in the beginning was the one doing the creating. So all seventy-two wrote it as God created in the beginning. In the legend, careful translation is a kind of guarding. And the rabbis had more than one feeling about it. In the Mishnah, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says that besides Hebrew, the holy books may be written in Greek. The Talmud finds a reason in Genesis, in Noah's blessing. In the King James words: "God shall enlarge Japheth, and he shall dwell in the tents of Shem." The rabbis read it as the beauty of Japheth, the Greek language, dwelling in the tents of Shem, Israel's house of study. But the minor tractate Soferim remembers a Greek translation made for King Ptolemy as a hard day, as hard for Israel as the day the golden calf was made, because the Torah could not be fully translated. Both memories sit in the tradition side by side. A gift that lets the Torah travel. A loss, because something always stays behind in the original. Anyone reading a verse in English today is standing inside the old Jewish argument about what that costs and what it gives.
screen: `ALL SEVENTY-TWO AGREE.` · `GOD CREATED IN THE BEGINNING.` · then, large: `GOD SHALL ENLARGE JAPHETH.` · `A GIFT, AND A HARD DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: read a verse in a translation. If you have a Bible or a phone nearby, pick one short verse, any verse. Read it once slowly in your own language. Then sit with it, and ask: which word here might be carrying something it can't quite hold? Which word would you want to see in the original? If you know a little Hebrew, look at the Hebrew too, and notice the difference without judging either one. If you don't have a verse at hand, use Noah's blessing from today. If you pray, you can use words from your tradition to give thanks for whoever carried this text into your language. The bell holds the time.
The Torah in Greek. Seventy-two elders in separate rooms, the Talmud says, and every one wrote the same words. Today's word.

Your line: the torah in greek. That ends a week that began with three parts, one library, then argued into the canon, plain meaning first, every word has a tune, the story continued, and two cultures meet. Today, thank one translator in your mind. Day eight hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Jews today read the Torah in Hebrew in the synagogue and study it in many languages, often with a translation printed beside the Hebrew; the Talmud's story of the seventy-two elders is taught in tractate Megillah.

original.note: Hebrew: the Greek language, the one tongue the Mishnah's Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel allows besides Hebrew for holy books.

trapdoor: what you thought: a translation is just the same book in another language.
what it means: the rabbis remembered the Greek Torah as both a gift and a loss: it traveled, and something stayed behind.

what a scholar hears: Megillah 9a tells of seventy-two elders in separate houses making the same changes; Megillah 9b grounds Greek in Noah's blessing of Japheth; Soferim compares the day to the golden calf.

notes: Claims rule: 'in Alexandria' from the outline was cut, since Megillah 9a names King Ptolemy but not the city. The number seventy-two is from Megillah 9a.
Megillah 9a: the first listed change is 'God created in the beginning' (Elohim bara bereshit). Please confirm the explanation offered in the teach is fair.
Megillah 9b reads Genesis 9:27 'yaft Elohim le-Yefet' as 'the beauty of Japheth' (Greek) dwelling in the tents of Shem. Please confirm.
Soferim 1:7 compares the day to the day the calf was made; Soferim 1:8 also gives the seventy-two elders story. Please confirm the ref.
